Structural basis of stepwise G protein activation by the viral chemokine receptor US28
abstract: Abstract G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) govern diverse cellular responses and are crucial drug targets. However, the sequence of structural events from G protein recognition to GDP release has remained elusive. Here, we leveraged the viral chemokine GPCR US28 to capture multiple activation states of the US28-G q complex. Using cryo-electron microscopy and an engineered chemokine superagonist, we determined three distinct complex structures, capturing a GDP-bound Encounter state, the nucleotide-free Canonical state, and a putative intermediate bridging the two states, the Transition-to-Canonical state. These structures, along with simulations and functional data, provide high-resolution snapshots of a plausible G protein activation trajectory and support a stepwise conformational model for G protein activation. This activation cascade closely parallels mechanisms proposed for human GPCRs, suggesting a conserved GPCR signaling mechanism.

The power of varying more than one thing at a time
abstract: Background Varying one thing at a time (VOTAT) is considered a universal approach for designing informative experiments. Its core idea is that controlled experiments can be designed by manipulating a single variable. However, we show that this single-manipulation heuristic can produce misleading evidence in contexts involving interrelated variables. We argue that varying more than one thing at a time (MOTAT) can be more informative when learners’ prior beliefs render alternative explanations implausible. Aims To test these claims, we compared single-manipulation to MOTAT experiments in a Bayesian learning simulation and a pre-registered empirical study on children’s learning about water displacement. Sample Participants in the empirical study were 185 children aged 6–9. Methods Learners predicted which of two spheres would displace more water and then observed an animation of the spheres being submerged. In the single-manipulation experiments, the spheres differed either only in size or only in material, leading to a confound of these dimensions with mass. In the MOTAT experiments, both size and material were manipulated such that the larger sphere was lighter. We investigated the formal informativeness of single-manipulation and MOTAT experiments (simulation study) and their effect on children’s learning, as measured via a post- and transfer test (empirical study). Results MOTAT experiments were most informative and led to the highest transfer test performance. Conclusion These findings provide initial evidence that VOTAT's core heuristic has a narrower scope than is commonly assumed. When variables are interrelated, deliberately varying more than one variable may be the better choice.
